An individual example illustrates what this distance means spatially (@fig-resection-localization b). In this patient, the peaks of both wCSET and sLORETA fall inside the resection at the half rising phase, as in `{python} resection_both_in` of the `{python} resection_n` patients. Only wCSET's peak was inside in `{python} resection_wcset_only_in` others, and only sLORETA's in `{python} resection_sloreta_only_in`.



## Study III: Clinical Dynamics (Simultaneous iEEG/EEG) {#sec-study3}

### Spatial Correlation Analysis

Study II scored a single location per patient. Study III instead tests how well each method reproduces the spatial pattern of activity recorded intracranially, across contacts and over time.

wCSET was compared against every other method at the timepoint level, on two sign-free measures: the amplitude rank correlation and the AUC (@sec-metric-corr, @sec-metric-auc), via the autocorrelation-corrected paired test of @sec-stats.

```{python filename="results_intra_vieeg_significance.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm
import pandas as pd

# Amplitude rank correlation (Spearman, |amplitude|) and AUC on |amplitude|, per subject, method and timepoint
# (processing_intra.qmd, "Spatial pattern metrics").
SPATIAL_DIR = "./results/intra/spatial_metrics"
vieeg_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load(SPATIAL_DIR)

# Subjects 12 and 50 (deep sources, far from the cortical source space) are reported in the Annex.
SUBJECT_ORDER = ["34", "48", "12", "50"]
MAIN_SUBJECTS = ["48", "34"]
SUBJECT_TITLES = {
    "34": "Subject 2",
    "48": "Subject 1",
    "12": "Subject 3\n(deep source)",
    "50": "Subject 4\n(deep source)",
}

# Competitor order matches processing_intra.qmd, whose cached statistics are reused.
COMPETITORS = ["sloreta", "cset", "dspm", "wmne", "beltrami"]
STANDARD = ["cset", "sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]  # GBF reported separately
VIEEG_METRICS = {"correlation_spatial_absrank": "amplitude rank correlation", "auc_spatial": "AUC on |amplitude|"}

# Per-timepoint values and cached test results.
vieeg_wide, vieeg_results = {}, {}
for metric in VIEEG_METRICS:
    for subject in SUBJECT_ORDER:
        wide = (vieeg_metrics.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"Subject": subject})
                .pivot_table(index="times", columns="Method", values="Value").dropna())
        vieeg_wide[(subject, metric)] = wide
        vieeg_results[(subject, metric)] = vieeg_metrics.stat.ttest_ess(
            metric, group_by="Method", comparisons=vieeg_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], COMPETITORS),
            pairing_col="times", subject_order=wide.index.tolist(), filters={"Subject": subject},
        )

# Statistics quoted in the prose: p-values and effects (positive = wCSET better) per competitor,
# and the per-timepoint differences wCSET - competitor behind each test.
vieeg_vs = {k: r.vs("wcset") for k, r in vieeg_results.items()}
vieeg_diffs = {k: vieeg_metrics.stat.paired_differences(r) for k, r in vieeg_results.items()}

def _median(subject, metric, method):
    return vieeg_wide[(subject, metric)][method].median()

_r, _auc = "correlation_spatial_absrank", "auc_spatial"

# Subject 1: wCSET vs. the four standard methods and CSET, then GBF.
_r48, _auc48 = vieeg_vs[("48", _r)], vieeg_vs[("48", _auc)]
_win48 = (vieeg_diffs[("48", _r)] > 0).mean() * 100  # % of timepoints where wCSET is higher
vieeg_48_r_wcset = fmt_num(_median("48", _r, "wcset"), 2)
vieeg_48_r_std_lo = fmt_num(min(_median("48", _r, c) for c in STANDARD), 2)
vieeg_48_r_std_hi = fmt_num(max(_median("48", _r, c) for c in STANDARD), 2)
vieeg_48_r_beltrami = fmt_num(_median("48", _r, "beltrami"), 2)
vieeg_48_spatial_p4_max = fmt_p(_r48.loc[STANDARD, "p_corrected"].max())
vieeg_48_spatial_dz4_lo = fmt_stat(_r48.loc[STANDARD, "effect"].min())
vieeg_48_spatial_dz4_hi = fmt_stat(_r48.loc[STANDARD, "effect"].max())
vieeg_48_winrate_min = f"{_win48[STANDARD].min():.0f}"
vieeg_48_winrate_max = f"{_win48[STANDARD].max():.0f}"
vieeg_48_spatial_p_beltrami = fmt_p(_r48.loc["beltrami", "p_corrected"])
vieeg_48_beltrami_winrate = f"{_win48['beltrami']:.0f}"
vieeg_48_auc_p4_max = fmt_p(_auc48.loc[STANDARD, "p_corrected"].max())
vieeg_48_auc_dz4_lo = fmt_stat(_auc48.loc[STANDARD, "effect"].min())
vieeg_48_auc_dz4_hi = fmt_stat(_auc48.loc[STANDARD, "effect"].max())
vieeg_48_auc_p_beltrami = fmt_p(_auc48.loc["beltrami", "p_corrected"])

# Subject 2: smallest p over every competitor and both metrics.
vieeg_34_p_min = fmt_p(min(vieeg_vs[("34", m)]["p_corrected"].min() for m in VIEEG_METRICS))
vieeg_34_r_wcset = fmt_num(_median("34", _r, "wcset"), 2)
vieeg_34_r_std_lo = fmt_num(min(_median("34", _r, c) for c in STANDARD), 2)
vieeg_34_r_std_hi = fmt_num(max(_median("34", _r, c) for c in STANDARD), 2)

# Signed Pearson correlation (Annex Figure 12), for comparison with Grova et al. 2016 and Afnan et al. 2026.
_signed = "correlation_spatial_signed"
_signed_vs, _signed_wide = {}, {}
for _s in MAIN_SUBJECTS:
    _w = (vieeg_metrics.to_df(metrics=_signed, filters={"Subject": _s})
          .pivot_table(index="times", columns="Method", values="Value").dropna())
    _signed_wide[_s] = _w
    _signed_vs[_s] = vieeg_metrics.stat.ttest_ess(
        _signed, group_by="Method", comparisons=vieeg_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], COMPETITORS),
        pairing_col="times", subject_order=_w.index.tolist(), filters={"Subject": _s},
    ).vs("wcset")
signed_48_wcset = fmt_num(_signed_wide["48"]["wcset"].median(), 2)
signed_48_std_lo = fmt_num(min(_signed_wide["48"][c].median() for c in STANDARD), 2)
signed_48_std_hi = fmt_num(max(_signed_wide["48"][c].median() for c in STANDARD), 2)
signed_48_p_max = fmt_p(_signed_vs["48"].loc[STANDARD, "p_corrected"].max())
signed_48_dz_lo = fmt_stat(_signed_vs["48"].loc[STANDARD, "effect"].min())
signed_48_dz_hi = fmt_stat(_signed_vs["48"].loc[STANDARD, "effect"].max())
signed_34_p_min = fmt_p(_signed_vs["34"]["p_corrected"].min())
signed_34_wcset = fmt_num(_signed_wide["34"]["wcset"].median(), 2)

# Glass-brain example (processing_intra.qmd): rho and top-contact overlap at the timepoint shown.
import json
_glass = {s_: json.load(open(f"./results/intra/glass_example/sub-{s_}.json")) for s_ in MAIN_SUBJECTS}
glass_n_top = _glass["48"]["n_top"]
glass_48_rho_wcset, glass_48_rho_sloreta = (fmt_num(_glass["48"]["rho"][m], 2) for m in ["wcset", "sloreta"])
glass_34_rho_wcset, glass_34_rho_sloreta = (fmt_num(_glass["34"]["rho"][m], 2) for m in ["wcset", "sloreta"])
glass_34_top_wcset, glass_34_top_sloreta = (_glass["34"]["top_overlap"][m] for m in ["wcset", "sloreta"])
```

In Subject 1 (@fig-intracranial-diff), wCSET's amplitude rank correlation with the recording (median ρ = `{python} vieeg_48_r_wcset`) was significantly higher than that of sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE and CSET (median ρ = `{python} vieeg_48_r_std_lo` to `{python} vieeg_48_r_std_hi`; largest p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_p4_max`, dz = `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_dz4_lo`–`{python} vieeg_48_spatial_dz4_hi`). wCSET was higher at `{python} vieeg_48_winrate_min`–`{python} vieeg_48_winrate_max`% of timepoints. The AUC led to the same conclusion (largest p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_auc_p4_max`, dz = `{python} vieeg_48_auc_dz4_lo`–`{python} vieeg_48_auc_dz4_hi`). Against GBF (median ρ = `{python} vieeg_48_r_beltrami`), neither metric differed significantly (rank correlation p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_p_beltrami`, AUC p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_auc_p_beltrami`), and wCSET was higher at `{python} vieeg_48_beltrami_winrate`% of timepoints.

Subject 2 did not reproduce this pattern: wCSET did not differ significantly from any other method on either metric (smallest p_corrected `{python} vieeg_34_p_min`). Median ρ was `{python} vieeg_34_r_wcset` for wCSET and `{python} vieeg_34_r_std_lo` to `{python} vieeg_34_r_std_hi` for the four other methods.

For comparison with @grova_intracranial_2016 and @afnan_assessing_2026, who report the signed Pearson correlation across contacts, we also computed that measure (Annex Figure 12). In Subject 1, it separated wCSET (median r = `{python} signed_48_wcset`) from sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE and CSET (`{python} signed_48_std_lo` to `{python} signed_48_std_hi`) more clearly than the polarity-invariant measures did (dz = `{python} signed_48_dz_lo`–`{python} signed_48_dz_hi`, largest p_corrected `{python} signed_48_p_max`). In Subject 2, it again showed no significant difference (smallest p_corrected `{python} signed_34_p_min`).


```{python filename="results_intra_vieeg_significance_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-intracranial-diff
#| fig-cap: "*Spatial agreement between virtual and recorded iEEG.* The two subjects with superficial sources (columns a, b); the two with deep sources are in Annex Figure 11. (a1, b1) Amplitude rank correlation per method at each timepoint of the comparison window: Spearman ρ across contacts between recorded and virtual absolute amplitude (box = IQR, line = median, outliers hidden; dotted line = 0). (a2, b2) Paired difference, wCSET minus each method, one value per timepoint (violin = distribution, thick line = median, thin line = IQR); positive = wCSET better. (a3, b3) Same for the AUC on |amplitude|: how well the virtual amplitudes identify the recorded active contacts (≥ 30% of the recorded maximum; 0.5 = chance). Above each violin: paired t-test with autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size (FDR-corrected), Cohen's dz, and the share of timepoints where wCSET is higher, minus 50% chance (e.g. +17% = higher at 67%)."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

VIEEG_ORDER = ["wcset"] + COMPETITORS

# Main-text subjects only; 12 and 50 are in the Annex.
vieeg_fig, vieeg_axes = plt.subplots(
    3, len(MAIN_SUBJECTS), figsize=(4.6 * len(MAIN_SUBJECTS), 12),
    gridspec_kw={"hspace": 0.6, "wspace": 0.3}, squeeze=False,
)
for col_i, subject in enumerate(MAIN_SUBJECTS):
    letter = "ab"[col_i]

    # (1) Spatial correlation per method, chance range shaded
    ax = vieeg_axes[0, col_i]
    vieeg_metrics.plot.group_comparison(
        vieeg_results[(subject, _r)], order=VIEEG_ORDER, palette=COLORS, points=False, showfliers=False, width=0.55,
        alpha=0, saturation=1, fill_alpha=FILL_ALPHA, chance_value=0,
        tick_labels=METHOD_LABELS, reference_suffix=" (ref.)", ax=ax,
    )
    plt.setp(ax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlabel("")
    ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude rank correlation (ρ)\nvirtual vs. recorded iEEG" if col_i == 0 else "", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(f"{letter}1. {SUBJECT_TITLES[subject]}: amplitude rank correlation per method", loc="left", fontsize=9)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

    # (2, 3) Paired differences per timepoint, positive = wCSET better
    for row_i, metric in enumerate(VIEEG_METRICS, start=1):
        dax = vieeg_axes[row_i, col_i]
        vieeg_metrics.plot.paired_differences(
            vieeg_results[(subject, metric)], reference="wcset", order=COMPETITORS, palette=COLORS,
            annotate=("stars", "effect", "winrate"), tick_labels=METHOD_LABELS, ax=dax,
            direction_labels=("wCSET better", "other method better") if col_i == len(MAIN_SUBJECTS) - 1 else None,
        )
        plt.setp(dax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8)
        dax.set_title(f"{letter}{row_i + 1}. {SUBJECT_TITLES[subject]}: {VIEEG_METRICS[metric]},\n"
                      "paired difference vs. wCSET", loc="left", fontsize=9)
        if col_i == 0:
            dax.set_ylabel(f"wCSET − method\n({VIEEG_METRICS[metric]})", fontsize=8)
share_ylim(vieeg_axes[0])  # per-method row comparable across subjects
```

@fig-intra-reconstruction shows one timepoint in detail: the peak of the virtual iEEG's global field power (GFP), averaged over the two methods. In Subject 1, wCSET and sLORETA both placed their largest amplitudes on the same left temporal electrode shafts as the recording, but mostly not on the same contacts within them (ρ = `{python} glass_48_rho_wcset` and `{python} glass_48_rho_sloreta`). In Subject 2, wCSET's largest amplitudes fell on the electrode shaft that dominated the recording, sharing `{python} glass_34_top_wcset` of its `{python} glass_n_top` strongest contacts, against `{python} glass_34_top_sloreta` for sLORETA (ρ = `{python} glass_34_rho_wcset` and `{python} glass_34_rho_sloreta`).

```{python filename="results_intra_spatial_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-intra-reconstruction
#| fig-cap: "*Recorded vs. virtual iEEG at one timepoint.* Subjects 1 and 2 (rows). (a1, b1) Intracranial global field power (GFP, standard deviation across contacts) of the recorded iEEG and of wCSET's and sLORETA's virtual iEEG, each scaled to its own maximum within the spike window (shaded); dashed line = the timepoint shown on the right, the peak of the averaged virtual GFPs. (a2–a4, b2–b4) Superior view with each intracranial contact colored by the rank of its absolute amplitude, from weakest (0) to strongest (1): recorded iEEG, wCSET, sLORETA. ρ = amplitude rank correlation with the recording."
import json
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Glass-brain renders and GFP curves from processing_intra.qmd
```

# Discussion

## Summary of Findings

We hypothesized that connectivity-informed methods would localize a source's onset about as well as standard methods, but reconstruct the co-activation patterns that follow more accurately (@sec-introduction). The three studies support both halves. In simulation and in the resection cohort, wCSET localized the onset about as well as the standard methods. In simulation, it reconstructed the subsequent co-activation patterns markedly better, and against simultaneous intracranial recordings it did so in one of the two evaluable subjects. A purely geometric alternative performed on par with wCSET throughout, and dMRI-free surrogate connectomes improved wCSET rather than degrading it.

These results also show why localization alone is an incomplete benchmark. Localization did not separate wCSET from the standard methods in either Study I or Study II, whereas measures of the spatial pattern of activity did, in simulation and in one intracranial subject. Each benchmark has its own blind spot: simulations are exact but rest on simplified models of the head, the spread of activity, and noise; resections are clinically grounded but spatially coarse; intracranial recordings are direct but sparse. Their agreement is what gives the results weight.

## Onset Localization and Co-Activation

At the quarter rising phase, wCSET localized the simulated onset about as accurately as CSET and dSPM, and more accurately than sLORETA and wMNE. The differences with CSET and dSPM were significant but small (r ≈ `{python} loc1_small_r`). They are bounded to one simulated subject and one set of sources, and their significance mainly reflects the `{python} simf_n_regions` regions behind each comparison. This is expected: connectivity information should help least while a source is still focal.

Its role becomes clear once activity spreads. From onset until `{python} corr1_window_end_lo`–`{python} corr1_window_end_hi` ms, wCSET's spatial correlation with the ground truth was higher than every other method's, and the gap with the standard methods was largest close to the peak. This fits a connectome spectrum that becomes more compact as activity spreads across connected regions [@rue-queralt_connectome_2021]. The advantage held down to an SNR of `{python} noise_corr_end_std` and under connectome corruption: wCSET never became significantly worse than sLORETA, even with every edge permuted, whereas CSET fell below sLORETA from `{python} deg_loc_cset_worse_start`% permutation on. This margin matters given how much false-positive structure real tractography contains [@maier-hein_challenge_2017].

The resection cohort gave the same picture for localization. wCSET's peak-to-resection distance was among the lowest (median `{python} resection_peak_median_wcset` mm, with GBF at `{python} resection_peak_median_beltrami` mm), and its peak fell inside the resection in `{python} resection_inside_wcset` of `{python} resection_n` patients (sLORETA: `{python} resection_inside_sloreta`). No comparison was significant, although every effect favoured wCSET (r = `{python} resection_r_lo`–`{python} resection_r_hi`). With `{python} resection_n` patients, differences as small as those seen in simulation would very likely go undetected, so this result is consistent with equivalent localization rather than proof of it. On the same cohort, @wang_geometry_2026 report a similar parity for GBF against dSPM, sLORETA, and eLORETA (P = 0.079–0.133), although GBF improved significantly over MNE (P = 0.012), which wCSET did not here.

Localization errors were larger here than in simulation (median `{python} resection_peak_median_wcset` mm, against `{python} simf_loc_trial_median_wcset` mm per simulated trial). This more likely reflects how real recordings differ from our simulation: real physiological noise is probably larger than our noise model assumes, and this cohort's data could not be whitened (@sec-data-resection). The cohort still answered the question it was included for. Localization against a resection is how the field conventionally validates these methods, and wCSET's co-activation advantage did not come at a cost in localization accuracy.

## Validation Against Intracranial Recordings

Simultaneous intracranial recordings offer the most direct test of the co-activation half of the hypothesis. We compared virtual and recorded iEEG with two polarity-invariant measures, the amplitude rank correlation and the AUC on |amplitude|. The polarity of an intracranial contact depends on its position relative to the generator and on the reference, which makes signed comparisons hard to interpret. For comparison with @grova_intracranial_2016 and @afnan_assessing_2026, the signed correlation (Annex Figure 12) led to the same conclusions, with larger effects.

Over the whole comparison window, wCSET outperformed sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE, and CSET on both measures in Subject 1, and did not differ from any of them in Subject 2. In neither subject was wCSET significantly worse than another method. The example of @fig-intra-reconstruction shows a single timepoint, the peak of the virtual GFP, at which wCSET agreed better with the recording than sLORETA in both subjects. In Subject 1, both methods placed their largest amplitudes on the right electrode shafts, but mostly not on the right contacts. In Subject 2, wCSET's largest amplitudes fell on the shaft that dominated the recording; this agreement did not persist over the rest of the window, hence no overall difference in that subject.

This advantage is relative, and absolute agreement with the recording was modest. On the signed correlation, wCSET's median over the comparison window was `{python} signed_48_wcset` in Subject 1 and `{python} signed_34_wcset` in Subject 2, within the 0.14–0.45 range that @afnan_assessing_2026 report between MEG and simultaneous SEEG at the spike peak. Agreement of this size appears inherent to this benchmark rather than specific to EEG or to our methods. Sparse sampling likely contributes: even with 67 to 146 contacts per subject, the electrodes sample only a small fraction of the cortex on which activity is reconstructed.

In the two subjects with deep sources, no method reconstructed the intracranial signal well, although wCSET outperformed CSET in Subject 3 on both measures. @grova_intracranial_2016 report the same limitation, which our cortically constrained source model cannot overcome (see Limitations).

## Connectome or Geometry?

A purely geometric alternative matched wCSET across all three studies. In simulation, replacing the true connectome with Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes, or with any other dMRI-free surrogate, did not degrade wCSET but improved it, for localization (r = `{python} loc_wcset_r_lo`–`{python} loc_wcset_r_hi`) and especially for spatial correlation at the peak (r = `{python} corr_wcset_r_lo_pp`–`{python} corr_wcset_r_hi_pp`). No surrogate stood out, and binarized surrogates, in which every edge has the same weight, performed like weighted ones. The benefit therefore rests on topology rather than on edge weights. In the resection cohort, GBF and wCSET had the lowest median distances, and against intracranial recordings neither came out significantly ahead in either subject. Using resected epileptogenic zones in 20 patients, @siu_structural_2026 found the same parity between geometric and connectome eigenmodes.

In practice, this is good news: wCSET does not need individual diffusion MRI, which is rarely acquired in clinical epilepsy workups. Studies II and III already relied on an atlas connectome.

Why would surrogates outperform the true connectome? We hypothesize that it comes down to how spatially concentrated each connectome's harmonics are (inverse participation ratio; Annex Figure 2). The true connectome's harmonics cluster on small, sometimes disjoint groups of dipoles, while the surrogates' harmonics spread more evenly across the cortex. Because wCSET's weighting makes the reconstruction lean on these harmonics, a clustered harmonic is a strong, specific bet: it pays off when activity is clustered the same way and backfires otherwise. The same trade-off appeared while designing wCSET. Weighting harmonics by their robustness to perturbation [@sipes_integrative_2024] favored very high-frequency harmonics, the most spatially focal ones, and introduced reconstruction artifacts; wCSET's smooth exponential decay avoids them.

What matters may therefore be less whether a connectome is anatomically true than whether its harmonics are spatially homogeneous. This would explain why Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes, which ignore white-matter connections entirely, still reconstruct well. It points to a limitation in how wCSET uses connectivity, not in connectivity information itself: its fixed weighting cannot tell whether a cluster it leans on reflects correlated activity or only the structure of the graph. CSET does not have this problem. Its sparse prior selects only the few harmonics that best explain the data, so it can leave out a clustered harmonic that does not match the activity, and it has little to gain from more homogeneous harmonics. Consistent with this, CSET showed small deficits with most surrogates. The exception was a large localization deficit with Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes (r = `{python} cset_beltrami_loc_r`): their leading eigenmodes are smooth, global patterns, so the few that a sparse prior selects may not be enough to place a focal onset.

## Limitations

Our source model restricts dipoles to a fixed-orientation, cortically constrained grid (@sec-source-space), which excludes deep and subcortical generators. This is why the two deep-source subjects of Study III could not be evaluated, and it is a missed opportunity: tractography, the very data our prior draws on, also encodes connections to and among deep structures. Including them would require encoding source orientation within the connectivity structure itself.

The regularization parameter λ was set by an SNR-derived heuristic (@sec-lambda) rather than tuned per subject or method. An exploratory sweep against the intracranial recordings suggested that the best value differs by about an order of magnitude across subjects, and neither generalized cross-validation nor the L-curve recovered a good value without ground truth. Principled, ground-truth-free selection of λ remains open for this method, as for any inverse method applied where no ground truth exists.

Our standard baselines were limited to methods available in MNE-Python. This excludes LORETA and LAURA, which @carboni_linear_2022 found most accurate for interictal spike localization, ahead of sLORETA and eLORETA.

Finally, only two intracranial subjects could be evaluated. Each subject's test accounts for autocorrelation across timepoints, but no test across independent subjects is possible, and more subjects are needed before these patterns can be generalized.

# Conclusion

Source reconstruction is conventionally benchmarked on localizing a single, focal generator, a criterion that says little about how well a method captures the co-activation of distributed regions. We introduced wCSET, which replaces CSET's sparse prior with a smooth, exponentially decaying L2 prior over the connectome-harmonic spectrum. We validated it alongside CSET, three connectivity-agnostic methods, and a geometry-based alternative (GBF) against three ground truths: a simulation of activity spreading across the structural connectome, the resected epileptogenic zone of seizure-free patients, and simultaneous intracranial recordings.

wCSET localized a source's onset about as well as the standard methods, in simulation and in the resection cohort. It reconstructed the co-activation patterns that follow markedly better in simulation, and against intracranial recordings in one of two evaluable subjects, without ever performing significantly worse than another method. This advantage held under moderate noise and considerable connectome corruption. dMRI-free surrogate connectomes even improved wCSET, so the method does not require individual diffusion MRI. A purely geometric alternative performed on par with wCSET in all three studies, as two independent groups also report [@wang_geometry_2026; @siu_structural_2026]. How evenly the harmonics spread over the cortex may therefore matter more than how anatomically accurate the connectome is.

Beyond wCSET itself, we see the three-part validation framework as the more lasting contribution: simulated, resected, and intracranial ground truths that together probe a source's full pattern of activity rather than its onset alone. Two of its parts stand on their own: a simulation in which activity spreads along the structural connectome in dipole space, and simultaneous EEG/iEEG recordings that test reconstruction beyond localization. Applying them to future connectivity- and geometry-informed methods, and to source models that include deep generators, are natural next steps toward source imaging that reflects the brain's network organization rather than reducing it to a single point.
